projectTitle: BMClick: One Shell to Click Them All
tagline: Bacterial microcompartment shells rebuilt outside the cell and made programmable by click chemistry, plus Ladder Detector, which annotates a gel in about a minute.
summary: BMClick rebuilds bacterial microcompartments (BMCs), the proteinaceous shells bacteria use to sequester metabolic reactions, in vitro and makes their surface programmable through click chemistry at an amber-codon-incorporated non-canonical amino acid, turning a natural containment system into a modular platform for working with purified biomolecules. The aim is to recover the organisation a cell provides, protecting therapeutic nucleic acids from nucleases, separating the steps of a reconstructed pathway, and extending the temperature and pH range over which enzymes work, while keeping the precision of in vitro conditions. The project also produced functional macroscopic materials from BMC-T shell proteins, and in vitro encapsulation was demonstrated with a HiBiT-SpyCatcher cargo and confirmed by cryo-EM. The dry-lab deliverable is Ladder Detector, a React + FastAPI web app that segments bands in a gel photograph using GelGenie's released U-Net models and then identifies which commercial ladder was run in the marker lane, a step no existing tool automated.

dry.frameworks: React web client plus a Python FastAPI server exposing a REST API documented as OpenAPI 3.1 (Ladder Detector API 0.1.0, Apache 2.0), with five endpoints split into a Segmentation group (GET /segmentation-models, POST /segment-image, POST /extract-band-details) and a Ladder group (GET /markers, POST /detect-ladder). There is deliberately no database layer: the application collects and stores no user data and keeps all configuration in files on the server. Deployment is Docker Compose with three services (frontend on 5173, backend on 8000, interactive API docs at /docs), and the segmentation models are pulled at build time from the GelGenie model registry on Hugging Face, so a HF access token is a prerequisite alongside Git and Docker.
dry.dataviz: The core output is the annotated gel image itself: upload a photograph, optionally crop or rotate, mark the marker lanes, and the app detects bands and writes the size labels on. Accepted input is PNG, JPEG, WebP and TIFF; the annotated result comes back as PNG. Where automation is imperfect the user gets real editing tools rather than a take-it-or-leave-it answer: a brush, an eraser and a magic wand for refining band detection, plus the ability to override the identified ladder or edit assigned values directly. A project can be saved and reloaded as a .gelproj file carrying the band segmentation and lane markup, and frontend and backend exchange JSON.
dry.datascience: The ladder-identification evaluation is the strongest part of the work. The team contacted Thermo Fisher Scientific for the band patterns of its DNA, RNA and protein ladders, scoped to six ladders their own lab uses, and then built a dataset of 172 marker-lane samples by combining their own gels, figures from published articles, and donated photographs solicited from the Vilnius University Life Sciences Center community and the organisers of the International Biology Olympiad. Because the algorithm is not machine learning but still has tunable parameters, they split 30% for parameter tuning and 70% for evaluation, used K-fold cross-validation within the tuning set, manually grouped samples that came from the same source or the same image so related samples could not leak across the split, and stratified by ladder. Four combinations were then tested on the held-out set: Dynamic Time Warping reached 52.42% (absolute run distance) and 62.90% (relative), while adjusted Needleman-Wunsch reached 89.52% and 91.13%. They published per-class tables, stated the two relevant baselines explicitly (about 17% for guessing one of six, about 26% for always guessing the most common class), and diagnosed their own failure case: Protein_6 was consistently confused with DNA_14 because both ladders have the same number of bands, so the gap penalties that normally separate ladders of different band counts provide no signal and only band positions remain. Relative run distance was chosen over absolute despite similar overall accuracy, because it handled Protein_6 better (61.9% vs 47.62%) and is the simpler of the two. Measured end-to-end annotation time is about one minute or less.
dry.software: Ladder Detector solves a real and unglamorous problem: gel annotation is done by hand, is repetitive and inconsistent, and the team found that although several gel-analysis tools exist, none automated the annotation step, even though almost every published gel figure is annotated. The pipeline has two stages. Band segmentation reuses rather than reinvents: GelGenie (Aquilina et al., Nature Communications 2025) showed that a lightweight U-Net and nnU-Net clearly beat classical Watershed and Multi-Otsu approaches, so Ladder Detector runs GelGenie's released models, defaulting to the Universal lightweight U-Net (seconds on an ordinary CPU) with nnU-Net and a sharp-band fine-tune selectable. Ladder identification is the team's own contribution, and the design decision behind it is instructive: their first idea was an image classifier over marker-lane crops, which they dropped after a consultation on two grounds, that they could not gather enough samples to train it reliably and that an image classifier would likely latch onto resolution, lighting or gel provenance instead of the band positions that actually distinguish ladders. They moved to numerical data instead, extracting band centroids from the segmentation mask and deriving absolute run distance (distance from the top of the lane) and relative run distance (normalised by lane height). The absolute approach exploits the empirical near-linearity of migration distance against log10(size): for each ladder in the registry, both sequences are min-max normalised, the log sizes inverted, aligned with an adjusted Needleman-Wunsch, a least-squares line fitted to the matched pairs, and the ladder scored by R-squared minus a penalty per unmatched band. The relative approach compares against per-ladder reference profiles taken from vendor charts and scores 1 - RMSE with the same unmatched-band penalty. The process flow deliberately keeps two human checkpoints, segmentation review and marker-lane selection, and the wiki explains why: segmentation is not always accurate, and when a gel has several marker lanes the app has no reliable way to tell which holds the ladder. The API exists specifically so the tool can become one step in an automated pipeline. It was deployed as a public web client at https://ladder-detector.onrender.com, which is the right instinct, but as of checking the service returns 'This service has been suspended by its owner', so the only working route today is self-hosting: 'git clone https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/vilnius-lithuania/ladder-detector.git', add a Hugging Face token to backend/.env, 'docker compose up --build'. Honest limitations are listed: only six ladders supported because of data availability, segmentation imperfect enough to need manual correction, and the classical identification approach possibly improvable by a trained model given a larger dataset. Licence Apache 2.0; it is described as a prototype.

good.publicEngagement: Education was rebuilt from scratch after a stakeholder told them their plan was wrong. The team had scouted a venue, contacted student organisations and planned to book a music band for one large science festival; Ieva Lingytė, a past team lead, warned them that a bigger event does not mean a bigger audience and that they should go to people rather than expect people to come to them. They scrapped it. The replacement framework borrows Ray Oldenburg's 'third place' sociology: home is the first place, university and formal events the second, and informal public spaces where people gather by choice (cafés, museums, clubs, shelters) the third, where status matters little and conversation is the main activity. Every event was then placed inside a community that already existed, with the format kept flat and walk-away-able for someone with no biology background who had not planned to meet science that evening: genetics discussed through the animals in the room at a cat shelter, fungi taught as a painting workshop ('Science Paints') at the MO Museum, and slots joined at the 'BŪTENT!' discussion festival and the VU Alumni Festival where the audience already existed. They iterated on format too, shortening and sharpening the questions for the second 'Science Talks' after the first showed people wanted more direct ones, and the discussion festival surfaced recognising fake science marketing as the topic people were most misinformed about. Separate consultations with Uršulė Barkauskaitė and Austėja Klevaitė specifically covered adapting activities for older adults, a group the team had no resources to involve meaningfully before.
good.ihp: More than 30 stakeholder meetings over 9 months, structured as open dialogue aimed at constructive criticism rather than presentation, with each insight systematically evaluated afterwards and failing approaches dropped. They named the loop the CLICK cycle (Consider, Listen, Implement, Check, Know your limitations) and published five values including Critical Reflection, which they define as examining their own baseline assumptions and being honest about limitations given that parts of the platform could have therapeutic value. Advice is mapped on an interactive timeline where every meeting records Description, Insights, Integration and Next steps, with three explicit revision points. Concrete redirections: alumni from the 2023 'Exullose' and 2025 'iXPOSE' teams set a realistic nine-month scope; the Kerfeld Laboratory advised on BMC assembly and protein modification; Prof. Rolandas Meškys shaped turning in vitro assembling BMC proteins into a modular platform; Dr. Yali Wang confirmed BMC-T functional material formation was possible after the team's own tests had repeatedly failed; critique from Ieva Lingytė (Biomatter Designs) and Dr. Juozas Nainys (Atrandi Biosciences) expanded a narrow thermostability aim into pH resistance testing and pushed them to find more creative applications, which produced the three-branch toolkit; and a consultation with Augustas Rinkevičius is recorded as 'Rethinking our ladder detection', the meeting that moved the software off an image classifier onto numerical band-distance matching.
good.realWorld: Commercial viability was reviewed with industry rather than assumed: Ieva Lingytė at Biomatter Designs and Dr. Juozas Nainys at Atrandi Biosciences reviewed and reprioritised the three project paths, Dr. Ignas Galminas took a pitch on the platform's commercial potential, Eglė Radzevičienė advised on intellectual property and industry realities, and the Vilnius University Innovation department ran a market analysis in October. Therapeutic plausibility of BMC shells as drug-delivery nanocarriers was checked with Prof. Aurelija Žvirblienė rather than claimed. The team also presented at the Nordic iGEM Conference.

gemsTakeaway: Build on the published model rather than training your own, and say why: Ladder Detector takes GelGenie's peer-reviewed U-Net weights for segmentation and spends its own effort on the one step nobody had automated, then rejects an image classifier on the explicit grounds that it would learn lighting and resolution instead of band positions. The transferable practice is their evaluation hygiene, a grouped and stratified split that stops samples from the same gel image leaking between tuning and test, stated random and majority-class baselines, per-class accuracy tables, and a published diagnosis of the one class the method fails on.
